title: Finish a wire splice: even the wire tips, then twist the connector on clockwise until snug
context: Electricians (about 800,000 US jobs, BLS) splice conductors in junction boxes as a core, everyday part of wiring work. The connector makers print it on every carton: strip the wires 16 mm (0.625 inch), hold them side by side with the tips even, and turn the twist-on connector clockwise until it is snug and no bare copper shows below its skirt. A wire whose tip sits short of the other is never gripped by the connector's coil, so it pulls out or arcs and heats the box; a connector that is only started is loose and leaves live copper exposed. Here someone has pushed the connector onto the tips by hand without turning it, and one wire has slipped back into the box, so only the other wire's tip is inside the connector.
setup: Positions are in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, with x forward, y to the robot's left and the table top at z 0. A galvanized steel junction box, 4-11/16 inches square (11.9 by 11.9 cm) and 5.4 cm deep, stands open face up, fixed to the bench, centered at x 30, y 0 (x 24.05 to 35.95, y -5.95 to 5.95). It has two screw tabs in opposite corners and a green ground screw on its back. Two black 12 AWG solid copper conductors with THHN insulation (3.3 mm across), short lengths not connected to any supply at either end (de-energized), come up through white plastic snap bushings (9 mm across) in two 6.4 mm holes drilled in the box's back: the right wire at x 24.7, y -3 and the left wire at x 35.3, y 3. Each rises straight up to 9 cm above the table, runs along x to x 30 at that height, then along y toward the middle, and stands up again at y -0.17 (right wire) or y 0.17 (left wire), so the two stand side by side touching at x 30. Each is stripped 16 mm at its end. The left wire is fixed (clamped under the bench): its insulation ends at 12 cm and its bare tip at 13.6 cm. The right wire starts 12 mm lower (insulation to 10.8 cm, tip at 12.4 cm, its horizontal runs at 7.8 cm); it can be drawn up or pushed down along its own length through its bushing and a rubber grommet under the bench that holds it where it is left (from 16 mm below the left tip to 10 mm above it). A red twist-on wire connector for two to four 12 AWG wires, 2.0 cm across its ribbed skirt, tapering to 1.2 cm at its rounded top, 2.8 cm long, with one white rib, sits loosely on the left wire's tip, its skirt at 12.8 cm, pushed on but not turned. Its coil is right-handed (it threads on clockwise seen from above). In the sim it travels 4 mm per turn, first bites 2.5 turns above snug, and is snug with its skirt at 11.8 cm, covering the last 2 mm of insulation (a real trial does not rely on these figures).
scoring: Doing nothing scores 0: the connector sits on one wire and nothing is spliced. In a real trial any way the robot turns the connector counts (gripped and rolled, or pushed round by a fingertip, either hand, any number of regrasps); only the outcome checks below decide the score. Once the robot has let go (if a gripper still holds the connector or a wire at the end, the operator opens it first), check in this order. Copper: look at the skirt from the side with a flashlight. Bare copper below the skirt is a shock and short-circuit hazard in a live box. Tug test: hang a 2 kg weight (about 20 N) from the right wire's end under the bench for 5 s, then pull the connector straight up with a spring scale to 20 N. 20 N is a firm hand tug, far more than the grommet's 2 to 3 N, so a wire the coil never gripped slides out, and far less than a gripped 12 AWG wire holds. The splice fails if a tape flag on the wire at its grommet shows it slid more than 1 mm (a gripped wire doesn't move; 1 mm is the least the flag shows plainly) or the connector comes off. Snug check: turn the connector clockwise with thumb and two fingers until it stops and count the molded ribs, 45 degrees apart, that pass a mark on the box. Scores: 0 if the splice fails the tug test: a wire that pulls out would arc and heat the box. 0.25: it holds, but copper shows. Both wires are joined, but it still needs fixing before the box is closed. 0.5: it holds and covers the copper, but turns more than one rib further. It is safe to touch, but a loose connector works off with heat and vibration. 1.0: it holds, covers the copper, turns one rib or less further, and both hands have let go, with no gripper touching the connector or either wire (checked in the final photo from the side), so the splice is seen to stay together on its own rather than held or pressed together by a hand; 0.5 if a gripper still holds it or a hand rests on it at the end, since the splice isn't shown to stay together on its own (the hand could be what keeps the wire in). A hand near the splice but off it is let go. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 1. Where the arms end up does not matter. Sim: the coil is a model, so the same outcomes come from proxies, read from the connector's angle back from its seat (where its skirt covers the last 2 mm of insulation) and the right wire's slide. Retained (the tug test's stand-in) = the right wire's tip within 3 mm of the left one's when the connector came a full turn on, 540 degrees back, and not moved over 2 mm since. 3 mm is under one 4 mm turn of the coil, so both tips enter its first turn. The sim's coil does not hold the wire, so a move over 2 mm after the bite counts as pulled out. Backing the connector off past that point judges it afresh, as an electrician would redo it. Copper shows more than 180 degrees back (2 mm of travel); snug is within 45 degrees (0.5 mm, one rib). 0 also if the connector is under a full turn on, or if more than 90 degrees of its turning on, net or clockwise in total, was not credited: the sim credits turning while a gripper grips the connector and turns with it (either hand, any regrasps, anywhere on its length), allowing 90 degrees for the slip between regrasps, because its coil holds the connector only lightly, so a push or knock could spin it on where a real one would not turn. Gripping = both fingers touching it with their opening stopped by its 2.0 cm width, not a hand merely near it. Held at the end (0.5 at most) = both fingers touching the connector or the right wire, their opening stopped by it. Touching = a gap of 2 mm or less (the solver's resting gap) between it and the gripper's own shape. Let go = no gripper touching the connector or either wire.
reset_notes: Turn the connector counterclockwise until it comes off. From under the bench, push the right wire down through its grommet until the paint mark on its insulation meets the grommet (tip 12 mm below the left one's), and set the connector back on the left tip, pushed on by hand but not turned. The left wire stays clamped. Nothing is used up.
fidelity: All parts are true size, and the wires are stiff: the left is fixed and the right only slides along its length, staying where it is left. The coil is a thread model: the connector is held on the wires' axis by a slide and hinge driven to 4 mm per turn, held by a light torque, stopped 60 degrees past snug. The wires do not twist together or turn. Retention, which a real trial checks with a tug test, is scored from the wire's position when the coil grips.
